li.a: Cathedral of St Michael and St Gudula, Brussels: History (archived 2019)
VRT NWS: Brussels Cathedral acknowledges stained-glass windows are anti-Semitic
Jewish Telegraphic Agency: Brussels cathedral installs plaques apologizing for medieval antisemitic persecution
Jerusalem Post: Brussels church removes antisemitic stained glass, apologizes for blood libel
European Jewish Congress: New plaque unveiled in the Brussels cathedral

content.p: In the Brussels cathedral, a set of stained-glass windows once showed Jews being burned at the stake for stealing and stabbing the consecrated bread of the Mass. For centuries the story was told as a miracle. The windows, the annual procession and a chapel of the host kept the legend alive in the city long after the people it accused had been killed or driven out. In April 2026 the cathedral's archbishop and the Chief Rabbi of Brussels unveiled plaques that call the accusation baseless and ask forgiveness from the Jewish people.

Several historical sources tie the affair to 1370 and to the same pattern of accusation. The Jewish Encyclopedia, writing in 1902, says that a banker of Enghien, known for his wealth and his charity, was murdered in his garden. His wife and son took refuge in Brussels. The assassins then spread the story that the Jews had taken consecrated wafers from a church and pierced them with daggers. The same encyclopedia dates the burning in Brussels to May 22, 1370, and says it was followed by a general banishment from Belgium.

Other sources give the start of the story differently. Its entry on host desecration lists the 1370 accusation at Enghien, and it does not say that the murder happened in Brussels. According to the Jerusalem Post, the affair began on a Good Friday in 1370, when at least six local Jews were suspected of taking consecrated bread and piercing it with a blade. In the legend, blood flowed from the wafers and was taken as a miracle.

The number of victims is the most disputed point. The 1902 Jewish Encyclopedia article on Brussels says the event led to "the burning of hundreds of Jews" in Brussels. The entry on host desecration, citing an 1870 article in the Revue belge, says that three Jews were burned in 1370 on the charge of stealing a host. The 2026 reports differ again. VRT reports that six Jews were executed in 1370 and burned at the stake in Brussels's market square. The Jerusalem Post says at least six Jews were accused. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency says some Jews were executed and others expelled. No single source settles the count, so each figure is given with the source that makes it.
content.h2: A legend turned into a festival
content.p: The wafer story did not end with the executions. According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, a great jubilee was celebrated in Brabant in 1820, lasting eight days, during which sixteen hosts set with diamonds were carried in procession through the streets. Brussels Cathedral's history says the miracle was venerated in the chapel that is now the cathedral treasury until shortly after the Second World War. The stained-glass windows showing the story were added in the 1900s, according to the Jerusalem Post, and they showed the Jews with caricatured hooked noses, according to VRT.

The Jewish Encyclopedia reports that in 1870, as Brussels clergy prepared for the festival, an article in the Revue belge titled "Le Jubilé d'un Faux Miracle" argued from the original sources that the 1370 record had been changed about sixty-five years after the event. The encyclopedia says that the altered wording was used to build a charge of desecration, and that Pope Pius IX felt obliged to stop the festival. That claim comes from the encyclopedia's account of the 1870 article. The 1870 article itself is not quoted here, so the claim is reported as the encyclopedia's account, not as established.

After the war, the Catholic Church's position on antisemitism changed. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reports that in 1969, shortly after the Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate declaration, the Archbishop of Brussels ordered that some paintings be removed and that a plaque be mounted. The cathedral's history dates the same step to 1968. A later plaque, inaugurated in 1977 by Cardinal L.-J. Suenens and placed in the former chapel, described the "tendentious nature of the accusation" and "the legendary portrayal of the miracle", according to VRT and the cathedral's history. The Brandeis scholar Flora Cassen, quoted by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, called the older plaque "very ambiguous about the responsibility" and said it was placed in an easy-to-miss location.

VRT reports that the 1977 plaque "drew considerable criticism from the Jewish community", who said it should have done more to remind people of the Catholic Church's own prejudice. VRT also reports that as recently as 2007 the Brussels historian Roel Jacobs noted that the cathedral could be regarded as one of the country's greatest antisemitic monuments.

On April 27, 2026, Archbishop Luc Terlinden of Mechelen-Brussels and Rabbi Albert Guigui unveiled four plaques in the Cathedral of St Michael and St Gudula, written in Dutch, French, English and Hebrew. The plaques state that "baseless accusations of the desecration of the Eucharistic host were made against Jewish communities" in medieval Europe, and that these accusations "led to persecution, massacres, and unjustifiable expulsions." They end with a request: "We ask forgiveness from the Jewish people for the suffering these accusations have caused." The Jewish Telegraphic Agency says the plaques cite the Nostra Aetate declaration and the 2000 statement of Pope John Paul II on the Church's responsibility for antisemitism.

Reports differ on the windows. The Jerusalem Post says the windows have been removed and the plaques installed. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency and VRT describe the plaques as context for the windows, which remain in place. The reports do not explain the difference, and this account does not settle it.

Flora Cassen said the new text was a "very moving" apology that "cannot be missed". Rabbi Guigui said in a statement that the plaques were an appropriate way to address relics of historical antisemitism. Archbishop Terlinden described the event as a new step in relations between Jews and Christians in Belgium.

The sources agree on the main outline: a rumour of desecration, the killing of Brussels Jews in 1370, and the expulsion of the community. Only the 1902 encyclopedia gives the murder that is said to have started the story. They disagree on the number killed, the place of the first accusation and the exact date. They also differ on how far the miracle was ever a matter of record. The 1902 encyclopedia and the 1870 article it cites treat the record as altered; the 2026 plaques call the accusation baseless. For the people accused, the lasting record is the banishment, the commemoration of the martyrs in Jewish memorial books and the centuries of procession and window art that repeated the charge.
